method_card.title: Pie Charts & Histograms
steps: Reading a pie chart: value = (share ÷ 100) × total
Equal class widths: the bar height is the frequency
Unequal class widths: frequency = density × class width
method_card.content:
Pie charts show parts of a whole. The full circle is 100%, or 360°, so a sector's angle is its share of one complete turn. To find what a sector is worth, take its share of the total.

Histograms show continuous data grouped into class intervals, so the bars touch. With equal class widths the bar height is the frequency. With unequal class widths the vertical axis is frequency density, and frequency = density × class width, which is the area of the bar.

Always check: sectors should total 100% or 360°, and class frequencies should total the sample size.
method_card.example:
Question: 120 people named their main transport: car 50%, bus 25%, walk 15%, cycle 10%. Find the car sector angle and the number of car users.

Angle: (50 ÷ 100) × 360 = 180°

People: (50 ÷ 100) × 120 = 60

gold.display: A country has 50 million people. The pie chart shows the employment structure. The government reports that 2 million people work in the primary sector. Is the pie chart accurate?
options: Yes, 2m out of 50m is 4%, which matches the chart
No, 2m out of 50m is 4%, but the chart shows 8%
No, 2m out of 50m is 2%, but the chart shows 4%

guided_steps.pre: Percentage the chart gives for the primary sector:

guided_steps.hint: Take one percentage away from the other.
guided_steps.done: A gap of nothing means the two agree, so the chart is not overstating or understating the primary sector.

guided_steps.say: The two figures agree, so the correct option is the first one: the chart is accurate.

guided_steps.hint: Multiply that bar's density by its wider class width.

guided_steps.hint: Multiply the tallest bar's density by its class width.
guided_steps.done: The tallest bar holds the same number as the low wide 30-50 bar, which is exactly why density must be multiplied by width instead of read as a count.

gold.hint: Turn each density into a frequency using its own class width before comparing them.
gold.display: Pebble sizes from a river were grouped into unequal classes and plotted as frequency density. The 0-5mm class has a frequency density of 4.0 and the 5-20mm class has a frequency density of 2.0. How many more pebbles were in the 5-20mm class than the 0-5mm class?

misconceptions.message: The densities have been compared directly. A density is not a count until it is multiplied by the class width.
misconceptions.note: expect derived by committing the error

misconceptions.message: The subtraction is the wrong way round. Check which class the question asks you to compare with which.
misconceptions.note: expect derived by committing the error

guided_steps.say: Densities cannot be compared directly. Turn each one into a count first.

guided_steps.pre: Width of the 0-5mm class, in mm:
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the lower class boundary from the upper one.

guided_steps.pre: Width of the 5-20mm class, in mm:
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the lower class boundary from the upper one.

guided_steps.pre: Frequency of the 0-5mm class (density times its width):
guided_steps.hint: Multiply that class density by the width you just found.

guided_steps.pre: Frequency of the 5-20mm class:
guided_steps.hint: Multiply that class density by its own wider class width.

guided_steps.pre: Subtract the smaller frequency from the larger:
guided_steps.hint: Compare the two counts you have worked out.
guided_steps.done: This is how many more pebbles the wider class held.

guided_steps.pre: Check: pebbles in the two classes altogether =
guided_steps.hint: Add the two frequencies.
guided_steps.done: The wider class holds more than half of the pebbles even though its bar is lower, confirming that density had to be multiplied by width.

problem_bank.bronze_description: Read one value straight off a pie chart or an equal width histogram, and turn a share into a pie chart angle
problem_bank.silver_description: Apply a share to a given total, or combine classes, moving between percentages, angles and real numbers
problem_bank.gold_description: Use frequency density with unequal class widths, and test whether a stated figure agrees with the chart

worked_examples.question: A pie chart shows land use in a village: farmland 50%, woodland 25%, residential 15%, other 10%. If the total area is 800 hectares, how many hectares are woodland?

steps.label: Read the frequency
steps.content: Since class widths are equal, the bar height gives the frequency directly: 18.

worked_examples.question: A histogram with equal class widths (0-10, 10-20, 20-30, 30-40) shows frequencies of 5, 12, 18, 8 for ages of visitors to a national park. How many visitors were aged 20-30?

bronze.title: Bronze: read a share straight off the chart
steps: A pie chart is one whole thing cut into slices. Each slice is labelled with its share, so reading one is really a matching job: find the label in the key, then read its sector.
A histogram with equal class widths is just as direct. The bars touch because the data is continuous, and the height of a bar is its frequency.
To turn a share into an angle, take it out of a hundred and multiply by 360, because a full circle is one whole turn.

example.question: A pie chart shows land use in a village: farmland 50%, woodland 25%, houses 25%. What angle does woodland take?

steps.label: Locate
steps.content: Find woodland in the key and read its share: 25%.

steps.label: Check
steps.content: Woodland is a quarter of the village, and 90° is a quarter of a full turn. ✓

silver.title: Silver: turn a share into a real number
steps: Silver questions hand you a total as well as a chart: a population, a sample size, a number of recorded events.
Read the share off the chart, divide it by a hundred, then multiply by the total. That gives the real number the slice stands for. Going the other way, an angle is (value ÷ total) × 360.
Two or more classes can be combined, but add the bars or the shares first, then do the arithmetic once.

example.question: A pie chart shows visitors to a park: adults 60%, children 40%. If 250 people visited, how many were children?

steps.label: Check
steps.content: Adults would be 150, and 150 + 100 = 250, the whole sample. ✓

gold.title: Gold: unequal class widths and testing claims
steps: When a histogram has unequal class widths the vertical axis shows frequency density, not frequency. A tall narrow bar can hold fewer items than a low wide one.
Frequency = frequency density × class width, which is the area of the bar. Work each class out on its own, then add or subtract.
Gold also asks you to judge a claim. Work out the figure the numbers give, then compare it with what the chart shows before you decide.

example.question: A histogram has classes 0-10 (density 3.0) and 10-30 (density 2.0). How many items are in the 10-30 class?

steps.label: Check
steps.content: The 0-10 class has the taller bar but only 3.0 × 10 = 30 items, fewer than the wide class. ✓

opener.label: Before any formulas
opener.display: A class of 24 students said what they had for lunch. Here is the result.

steps.say: No method needed yet. Just look at how much of the circle each choice takes.
steps.hint: Chips fill half the circle, and there are 24 students in the class.

steps.say: You did that by size, not by counting. A slice's share of the circle is its share of the class.
steps.pre: Degrees of turn the chips slice takes:
steps.hint: All the way round is 360°, and chips take half of that.

steps.say: That is the whole technique. A pie chart turns a share of a group into a share of one full turn, so half the class becomes half the circle, which is 180°. Read it forwards to get an angle, or backwards to get a number of people. A histogram does the same job for measurements grouped into ranges: it is the size of the bar, not its label, that carries the number.

bronze.label: Together: your first one
bronze.display: The pie chart shows land use on a farm. What percentage is barley, and what angle does that sector take?

steps.say: Locate before you read. Start by seeing how the chart is split.
steps.pre: Land uses shown in the key:
steps.hint: Count the entries listed beside the chart.

steps.pre: Counting down the key from the top, barley is at position
steps.hint: The key runs wheat, barley, grass, woodland.
steps.done: Found the slice first. Most pie chart marks are lost here, not in the arithmetic.

steps.hint: Read the share written next to barley in the key.

steps.say: Now the new move: turn that share into an angle. A full pie chart is one complete turn of 360°.
steps.hint: Divide the percentage by a hundred.

steps.pre: Multiply by 360 for the angle in degrees:
steps.hint: Take that fraction of a full turn.
steps.done: A quarter of the farm, a quarter of the circle.

steps.say: Check it against the rest of the chart:
steps.pre: Total of all four percentages in the key:
steps.hint: Add wheat, barley, grass and woodland.
steps.done: The shares make a whole 100%, so barley really is a quarter and 90° is right.

silver.label: Together: adding the total
silver.display: 400 shoppers said where they buy most of their food. How many use a market stall?

steps.say: Same start as bronze: find the slice on the chart before touching the total.
steps.hint: Count the entries listed beside the chart.

steps.pre: Counting down the key from the top, the market stall is at position
steps.hint: The key runs supermarket, online, market stall, corner shop.
Read the share written next to the market stall.

steps.say: Here is the silver move: the chart gives a share, the question gives a total. Put them together.
steps.hint: Divide the percentage by a hundred.
Take that fraction of everyone surveyed.
steps.done: The share has become a real number of people.

steps.say: Check by doing the biggest slice the same way:
steps.hint: Take the supermarket share of the same 400 shoppers.
steps.done: 180 supermarket, 100 online, 80 market and 40 corner shop rebuild all 400 shoppers, so the shares were applied correctly.

gold.label: Together: when the widths differ
gold.display: This histogram has unequal class widths, so the vertical axis shows frequency density. How many pebbles are longer than 20mm?

steps.say: Locate first. Look at the horizontal axis and see how the classes are split, because they are not all the same width.
steps.hint: Count the blocks along the horizontal axis.
The classes run 0-10, 10-20, 20-40 and 40-80.
steps.done: Two classes to work out, and they are different widths, which is the whole point of this tier.

steps.pre: Width of the 20-40 class, in mm:
steps.hint: Subtract the lower class boundary from the upper one.

steps.say: Now the gold move: frequency = frequency density × class width. The bar's area is the count, not its height.
steps.hint: Multiply that bar's density of 1.5 by the width you just found.
That class is 40mm wide and its density is 0.5.
Combine the two counts you worked out.
steps.done: This is the number longer than 20mm.

steps.say: Check against the tallest bar on the chart:
steps.hint: Multiply that bar's density by its class width.
steps.done: The tallest bar holds fewer pebbles than the two low wide bars together, which is exactly why height alone cannot be read as a count.
